utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good afternoon Your Honours, this is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Very well. This is Wednesday and I welcome the witness, Ms. Dahl, Mr. Seselj and each and everyone in this courtroom. We are now to continue with the cross-examination. The Accused so far has used up 1 hour and 26 minutes. Prosecution had used 5 hours and 32 minutes; therefore, the Accused still has 4 hours and 6 minutes for the cross-examination. Mr. Seselj, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, we never met directly, you and I, before?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We never spoke to each other, did we, as far as I could recollect?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I think we shook hands several times. When in a crowd of many other people when I shook hands with lots of other people, that was probably it but we never talked, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said. When you came to Sid we shook hands in the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, according to your answer during the examination in chief, you went to the Herzegovina battlefield with Vakic in 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not literally with him. Actually, he was already there before me, and as far as I heard from him he took over the unit from Oliver. And afterwards with a group of volunteers I went to Belgrade, I asked Pasilovic [phoen] or someone else for an accompanying letter inviting, or rather asking for state transport vehicles so that we wouldn't have to pay money for reaching our destination, so I was a little late. He was already there when I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you had free transport, right, because you were volunteers?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were given a letter to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I see. Now Vakic with his volunteer unit was included straight away into the unit of the army of Republika Srpska, right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely correct. On a daily basis as commander he would go to Trebinje for discussions every morning, and sometimes I'd go with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You mean for reporting?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And he would be told on that particular day what his unit was supposed do?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Tasks, guidelines, food, everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you were at Grabinje -- Trebinje, right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Grab is a military facility. It's a forward, I think it was called a forward military facility or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, your task to begin with was to guard the border area of Trebinje facing Dubrovnik; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only to guard it but to reconnoiter and do reconnaissance work as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Ljubo Ivanovic, nicknamed Ljubo Chetnik, was the head of a platoon or a squad, is that right, of reconnaissance men?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He arrived later on with a group of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He joined up with Vakic, did he?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the same facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Branislav Vakic will be a Defence witness. So he provided you with quite a bit of information. He says that Ljubo Ivanovic had the task of supervising the area which is called Bobanj.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Following the cross-examination on statements yesterday by the accused who had collected these materials and gave them to us, I'd like to point out the Chamber's prior decision on proper cross-examination. If the Accused or myself for that matter, wishes to cross-examine a witness, under the Trial Chamber's guidelines, it is inappropriate to put to the witness the source of the information being conveyed, and I'd refer to paragraph 26 of the 15 November 2007 order in which the Chamber states: "The party cross-examining a witness may show the witness the information obtained from a previous on the condition that the source of the information is not identified." I would suggest that a reasonable interpretation of that direction includes not telling the witness, I heard this from so and so, did he tell me right, or is it correct that that information that I got from so and so is true? In this instance Mr. Seslj has volunteered to the witness an individual who will be called -- whom the Defence intends to call as a witness as the source and then asked the witness questions concerning that information. I believe that violates the Chamber's guidelines on cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have something to say. I think that this is an unreasonable interpretation by Ms. Dahl. Not a reasonable one because your ruling referred to the previous witnesses which have already testified in Court. And before Mr. Stoparic, we just heard expert witness Oberschall. Now, I'm talking about someone who is the commander of a unit in which Mr. Stoparic was himself at the Herzegovina battleground, and I do have the right to mention his name and what he says about it. It's not a violation of your guideline and ruling because I'm not mentioning any previous Prosecution witnesses and then asking the witness to comment on what anyone of them said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I do not have this ruling before me. I'm going to be given it by a legal officer, but you are entitled to speak about his commander. However, you could have avoided saying that he was going to be one of your witnesses, because if you do so -- as you did so you are creating a situation which should not be taken into account by the witness. He doesn't need to take into account whether his chief was going to be a Prosection or Defence witness, but proceed please. THE ACCUSED SESELJ: I think Mr. President, that there is nothing more natural than for Branislav Vakic and other people that I proclaim to be Chetnik Vojvodas for the things they did in the war, to come in as Defence witnesses. Secondly, he won't be a protected witness. I'm not going to have a single protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I agree with you. You can choose your witnesses as you please, but you do not want to induce a specific behaviour to a witness. No need to tell him that that man is going to testify after he does because if you do so, you pressurize him. He may well think, Well, if I say something the other one might think or say the opposite. So this is not to your advantage technically. No need to tell this witness that somebody is going to come and testify who might contradict what this witness says because if you do so, you pressurize the witness. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, Ljubo Ivanovic was the commander of a squad as we said which took part in reconnaissance work in the are that was called Bobanj; that is to say between Popovo Polje and the sea. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally knew Ljubo Ivanovic, and I do know that he came to Grab. Now, whether the place is called Bobanj or not I'm not quite sure, but I'm almost certain that he spent one or two nights in Grab we were all the time so that I considered that he was a separate unit working for the same interest. Now, please believe me when I say I was promoted to Mr. Vakic's deputy, but through the documents that I kept, that meant manpower, procurement of resources, and anything more serious with the negotiations of the coming -- Trebinje, that's what Mr. Vakic did, if I can put it that way. Although, he didn't hide anything from me so that it is possible that he was our forward department in a way. So perhaps I knew this, perhaps I didn't. I see no reason not to say that he was there because we were there for the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Ljubo Ivanovic was a JNA soldier in the fighting in Slovenia, do you know that, in 1991?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ljubo Ivanovic, in the first two actions was in Leva Supoderica as well. I think he was -- that. A very brave guy was killed by the name of Vlada Lukic in that first operation. Later on every unit that was led by Mr. Ivanovic, he would call the unit Vlada Lukic in memory of that man.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Ljubo Ivanovic was already prominent and known as a courageous and brave fighter, right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have seen many fighters, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He was famous among the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was among the top 12, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Ljubo Ivanovic, carried by this fame of his, just could not accept Branislav Vakic being an authority above him; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't remember that, but between the two of them there was a conflict of interest. That is true, and you've just reminded me of that. Quite simply Ljubo Ivanovic, at least that's what I think, and it's not nice to speak ill of the dead, ever, but he thought that he knew more and knew better than Vakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And there was this tension constantly towards Vakic, his tension towards Vakic.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as I say, there was a conflict of interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And at one point Ljubo Ivanovic separated from Vakic and left the unit with a group of fighters; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just waiting because I'm waiting for the interpretation. I know that Ljubo Ivanovic was at another post and that sometimes he would sleep where we were. But the conflict wasn't that they hated each other, at the time officially there was this other unit, another group of volunteers and he was with them. But I can't-- I'm not quite convinced of that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Ljubo Ivanovic left Vakic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry for interrupting you. I have the ruling now in front of me. I'm going to read paragraph 26 of the said ruling: "The cross-examining party can confront the witness with information obtained from a previous witness provided the identity of the source is not identified." This is what you reminded us, Ms. Dahl, but if you have a strict reading of this paragraph, when it says a pervious witness in my mind, that is a previous witness who has testified. If a witness has testified, indeed the accused can say to a witness, Somebody came here to testify, I don't give you the name, who said, for instance, there were three trucks. You said there were two. Who's right? That's how it should take place. So when it says here "previous witness" this is not about a witness whose testimony is not even known.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I agree with the notion that one should not disclose the source of a previous witness' testimony, but I think that the principle embodied in this is that the prior testimony has an assurance of accuracy because it has been put before the Chamber under the supervision of the Chamber and under an oath or affirmation as to its truthfulness, that imbues the testimony with some quality that makes it worthy to challenge the current witness with discrepancies and to confront a current witness with it. The bringing forth of information derived from someone who has yet to make an appearance before the Chamber is of a lesser quality. And it may be that the individuals that Mr. Seselj has gathered his information from do present themselves to the Chamber for examination, but it compromises as you've said before or puts pressure on the current witness to bring in un-tested information and attribute it to the source in order to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, the problem is that you're both right. We can have the following situation: Let me go back to this example with three or two trucks. Let us imagine that a witness said I saw three trucks. Mr. Seslj has his own Defence witness, and he knows because he was told so by his investigators that that witness had two trucks. So in this case, in this very hypothetical case, Mr. Seselj could say, Well, witness, you said that you saw three trucks. I have a witness who says that he saw two. So he can test the witness without giving the name of that other witness of course. So really on a case by case basis you're both right, but it is really on a case by case basis you're right to say that when a witness has made a solemn declaration, what he says might be relevant and it can be tested, confronted with what another witness says here. But here we have a case where this -- that other witness has not testified yet. So the Trial Chamber does not know him at all, but the Defence knows that on this or that point there may be a contradiction between that other witness and this one. So the accused can say I have information that enabled me to say that what you say here may not be right. So then he has an answer from this witness, and later on when that other witness comes to testify you can always cross-examine him or her.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me suggest that the purpose of cross-examination can be achieved simply by asking the witness: Weren't there two trucks. And then if the witness denies that he's been confronted with the information and is not contaminated or pressured with the idea that a hundred other people who saw the accident said there were two trucks because that really isn't the point of confronting the witness with how many witnesses disagree with him so much as what is his recollection of the facts to which he is testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, you have the floor again. So far you mastered the technique of cross-examination. I know that you conducted several investigation committees and that you know very well what the procedural rules are. Please take our rulings into account, take into account the current discussion and do your best. If ever there's a problem, we'll have an objection by the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber will settle the matter. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have to note that Ms. Dahl said something nebulous, something that I have never heard before. Let me remind you. She said that the testimony of previous witnesses are considered to be correct because they took the solemn declaration and so on. That is all nebulous. Now, when the proceedings are over it is up to you as the Trial Chamber to assess what testimony was true, what was not, what was more true, less true or what the testimony was like anyway. So it's not the order of witnesses testifying that determines whether a testimony is correct or not. I never thought that I would hear anything like that said in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did hear what she said, but I believe that she meant to say that a witness who has made a solemn declaration, such as this one, when they say something it has a certain value. The fact that they testify under oath carries automatically with it that it is imbued with a certain value. It is not necessarily the truth but it has a certain value. I think that was the meaning of what Ms. Dahl said. But let's move on to other questions now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, let's now make a slight digression here. Do you consider when somebody says in this courtroom, I take the solemn declaration, I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth that that is a true oath, just the same as when the oath is, I solemnly swear, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you say "swear," that is binding.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's a proper oath.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In Serbian legislation in Serbia and in the army that's what it is like. Now this is a solemn obligation, this declaration, and I accepted it and I know that I am quite responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm not asking about you, but abstractly.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When somebody says, I hereby declare, doesn't that remind you of our primary school in the pioneers movement of children there when we pledged to our dictator Tito?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did the same when I was a pioneer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And then we made jokes on the subject later on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Mr. Seselj. Indeed, you have tackled this issue in other hearings. Witness, you have taken an oath, you read the text of it, but we are privileged because we know that -- we know that you have been a witness before other courts, including national courts. There too you took an oath. So do you make any difference in your mind between testifying before domestic judges or before international judges? Is there a difference or not in your mind, or does the oath that you took, the solemn declaration, does it have the same value?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In a way here, it's a little differently constructed, but as a man, as a human being if I read it out, then, to a certain extent I consider that I have sworn, as I would in Serbian, so I'm conscious that I can -- that legal proceedings can be taken against me for every word that I say that is not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... That the three Judges you have in front of you would be domestic judges, would that change anything to the answers you give to Mr. Seselj's questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I do not wish to change my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was important to testify there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I just wish to impress upon the Court that no one among the Serbs, Croats, Albanians, Muslims and Macedonians who appear before this Court to testify do not one of them consider this solemn declaration to have the strength of an oath. An oath is a sacred act. When -- this reminds all the people of the communist times when actually one cracked jokes about solemn declarations. Solemn declarations would be used in the pioneers league which was the communist organisation of the youngest and in the communist army of the former Yugoslavia. This is what I wish to say and now I shall proceed with my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So I have impressed it upon you that according to my information Ljubo Ivanovic, with a group of combatants, left Vakic's unit and then headed in the direction of Mostar. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know in which direction he went.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, he appeared eventually in the Borackori Lake and this is where he was killed, right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when he was killed. I believe but it doesn't have to be true, he may have been by Boracko Lake, but he may have taken a furlough and gone home and then he reappeared at Boracko Lake but it doesn't have to be exact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But he died near Boracko Lake in Bora Antelj's unit. Did you hear about Bora Antelj?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have heard about that name, that of Bora Antelj, but I don't know where exactly he got killed, but I did go to Nis to his funeral.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You said that a message of mine was read out there at that funeral. Could that have been a cable, a telegram?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a telegram.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, it could only have been a cable because I could not sent a letter because the funeral took place after a very short while. So it was a telegram with my condolences to the family on account of the death of Ivanovic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You offered your gratitude for his contribution to the fighting. It was a telegram offering your condolences and I don't know whether it indicated that his promotion --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: No, posthumously, no, but he was promoted to any rank.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't agree. There had been posthumous promotions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, in history, but not when I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true, Mr. Seselj. I thought that that may have been the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why am I saying this? I cannot find it in the records of the Serbian Radical Party that I sent any telegrams then because we meticulously record all our public appearances, but it is possible because although he had left the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party and joined another unit that we had nothing to do with, I remember another case. Have you heard -- had you heard about Mirko Lavadinovic, Uca?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Uca rings a bell, but I don't know whether that's that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mirko Lavadinovic, Uca, is from Belgrade, and he was a volunteer of the Serbian Radical Party in villages, Slavonian villages north of Vukovar, and as our volunteers would go there to the front for about a month, and they would go home for a rest, for a furlough, when his group left for home, he remained. He stayed on and joined Arkan's unit, and he got killed as a member of Arkan's unit. And irrespective of the fact that he had abandoned the Radical Party volunteers, it is my opinion that he got killed in defending the Serbian people and I went to attend his funeral, because I consider that to be my morale obligation. I knew him, I knew that he got killed fighting for the freedom of his people, and at that funeral I also met with Arkan, although we had a long-standing animosity obtaining between us and sometimes overt hostilities so I do not rule out the possibility that I sent a telegram to the family of Ljubo Ivanovic, but by that time he had no longer been our volunteer or our member.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. This is a statement. This is not a question. You should have said, Witness, did you know that I sent a telegram, that I went to the funeral. Then he would have answered yes or no. But you're testifying right now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was just about to ask that question, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The fact that I sent -- possibly sent this telegram, can it be treated in this way: I knew him, I knew that he had been killed at the battle front and regardless of the fact that he had parted ways with our volunteers, I paid a certain tribute to him?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, had that been not so, would you have had any volunteers in the period after that at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you think that what I'm saying is plausible or do you think that it was so?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see no reason why he shouldn't be honoured for the period in which he fought, even if he was a member of another unit, he was on the Serbian side in a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did not join the national guards?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stoparic, Vakic at Grab was given the orders to go to the area between Nevesinje and Velez with his unit at Podvelezje?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is Podvelezje, it's called Podvelezje. This is a plateau. It is quite high ground in respect of Nevesinje. It is quite forbidden terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And that was of strategic importance for the Serbian army?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And Vakic was issued orders to penetrate Muslim positions and take Podvelezje, right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What happened in the terrain, we were the striking fist of what was going on. There were also armoured resources and other units participating but we were the striking fist of that penetration.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the parties please not overlap.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You were there during that operation?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to say that it was not the entire unit that went there. We didn't have enough transport means but the number of people who could be transported by what means we had and that group was divided by Vakic into two parts. He led one group and I was in charge of the other group so that the path which was the coordination which was actually the axis of our operation, I was on the left side of that road and Mr. Vakic was on the right side in or advance towards enemy forces but we communicated via radio of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Before you put in an attack you had artillery support, did you not?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the standard artillery preparation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How long did that last? Was strong?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But it was strong?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. There was also friendly fire, casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you put in an attack and our artillery had not stopped with its fire at -- yet?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the system which is usually applied. The artillery stops after five minutes and then the infantry advances attacking and as we were trained and we exceptionally courageous, we wanted to advance and to approach the enemy as -- to be as near him as possible during the artillery preparation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you succeeded in defeating the enemy and taking his positions?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found out about the success of the action in hospital because I was among the first who got wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In view of the artillery preparation there certainly were no civilians in those villages?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm always inclined to say civilians were there only in the very beginning of the war when not even our enemy knew how to conduct himself, how to comport himself, but later in the second year when everybody had formed their armies and the JNA was in the withdrawal stage, at that point in time if the front line was a village, all these civilians would have been moved by the respective sides in order for them to avoid being exposed to danger, so I'm sure that at that point there were no civilians. If there were any, they would have remained there on their own initiative.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes. So were combat actions, I expected where there is already artillery preparation, the civilians whether they are Muslims, Serbs or Croats are evacuated.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is quite normal procedure only in the very beginning at the very beginning of the war something different could have happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But this was well into the war, right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So it would be folly to expose one's own civilians to enemy fire, to one's own fire?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, many times I was in charge of the artillery weapons and fired it myself and I never had the intention of firing at any targets which I did not consider to be military targets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, Mr. Seselj is addressing very technical and very military aspects. There's no problem, but you just confirmed that you had directed artillery fire. That seems that you also are very component in this respect. When artillery is shooting, and when the -- the people know that there are civilians, are they supposed to shoot and fire on houses where they know that there are civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tried to explain, Your Honours. To direct artillery fire in the Serbian language means to be a direct combatant at the very line of contact with the enemy and to also be in charge of adjusting the fire, so I was directing the weaponry fire and using the fire-power of the heavy military hardware. Of course, I, as a soldier, at the very front line, had no reason whatsoever to bomb or to shell or to have the commander of the artillery unit shell a target which I need not -- needed not to have destroyed. What I needed was to prepare the field by artillery fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... Well, but in what you're saying obviously there's two elements. There's a reconnaissance group that is going to recognise where the targets are and then this group will give an order to the artillery men to fire. But if the reconnaissance group notices or finds out that there are civilians, what happens then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That group would immediately report back to the command, inform the command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what would happen next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Usually the reconnaissance group, and I used to be the leader of such a group, the commander, would seek out a target. If we are talking about simply reconnaissance without combat action. I just locate a target for a future action. But we are talking about combat actions, ongoing combat actions themselves, then you don't have the possibility to target civilians with artillery fire, nor is that the objective. You just try to direct your fire to targets which are facilities from which fire is received. So military facilities, in a nutshell. I cannot say that at times a school was not a military facility. Sometimes it would be a pill box, a nest, a machine-gun nest and used as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's take a simple example. Imagine there is a village, in this village there is enemy forces either are in or around the village. But in the village there are also women, children, elderly people who stayed in the village. What should the reconnaissance group and what should the artillery group do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it is our objective to attack that village and take the area and we know that there are civilians in it, several days prior to our action we reconnoitre the area and we identify the actual targets and we shell the front lines. The front lines are usually 300 metres away from the first row of houses, and the second line of enemy's positions is in the first row of houses usually there -- there are no civilians there and it is not logical for civilians to be there. They are in the rear of the village, which we never shell but we do shell that part of the village once we have advanced to the front part of the victim but by that time the civilians will have been evacuated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: According to information Mr. Stoparic was a single Muslim civilian killed during the attack at Podvelezje. Do you know that any Muslim got killed?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a fact which I have repeated many time and it is absolutely true. I, as a Serbian soldier, in uniform, whether I call myself a Chetnik or not, that is of no consequence, and whether I came there organised by the Radical Party or some other organisation or the police, I have a uniform and I'm a clearly identified person. I have the patch identifying me clearly and that is of course because the enemy can have similar or identical uniform and I needed to be identified. But it was very difficult to distinguish a civilian from a soldier at that time in those years. There were many instances of a civilian killing or wounding somebody because he was also armed. In fact I myself was later wounded in Kosovo because I failed to react efficiently to a civilian who was ten metres away from me and took out a Kalashnikov and almost killed me. Sometimes it was very hard to make this distinction but I don't know of any case of somebody actually shooting, executing a civilian on purpose, and when the artillery was active and the riflemen were active this is the same thing, the same practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: If I understood you well, not all the Muslim soldiers at that time wore uniforms, had uniforms?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: They were not provided with enough uniforms.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said it was difficult even in the thick of battle to make a distinction between a civilian and a soldiers. At a certain point of time I would notice a piece of weaponry and civilians arms and at that moment that person was no longer a civilian to me but I have to approach him to a distance of some ten metres in order to be able to identify the difference. We never had any members of our unit that were in civilian clothes. In Mufti they could have sweatsuits on when they were not in combat but not in combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: During your actions was a body of a Muslim woman or a child found? And I'm speaking about Podvelezje. You finished your combat action, you took the Muslim positions in Podvelezje, you conquer them and then did you find out whether a child or a women had been killed?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When? What was the target, the objective of our action was achieved when we took that area. I was in hospital, in Nevesinje in a makeshift hospital so that I did not have the honour to actually celebrate the successful action because I had been wounded but nobody informed me of any such case. I don't know that that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But had it happened would you have been informed, do you think?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, immediately. After the cessation of the combat actions it was not only I who was wounded among Vakic's men. There were others and there is a list of the wounded and dead. In fact, a soldier committed suicide. This is not indicated in the list because he was so severely wounded we tried to evacuate him. We established visual contact with him but he activated a grenade and committed suicide. It was our practice not to indicate this in our reports. We did not want Milosevic's regime to create any problems for us on that account.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It is it stated here, it was slipped in, in -- in your statement. The question of this unit so that one could draw the conclusion that there were three units of volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party at the same time. One was led by Vakic, the other by Oliver Denis Barret and the third by Ljubo Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I'm quite absolutely certain that Vakic took over the Grab facility from Oliver Denis. He was withdrawn back to Belgrade and the other one continued. Yes, Ljubo Ivanovic stayed on with his unit which he called Chetniks, but he was always a Chetnik. At the same time it is impossible for them to have been there -- well, Denis had already been withdrawn. So I don't believe that I ever said that it was at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to hear from you. Very well. Because what I'm doing is refuting what they made you sign here. Mr. Stoparic, do you know why Oliver Denis had to leave the unit?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I don't know whether he is the only one who left the unit. Maybe he withdrew all the men who were under his command and Vakic maybe came in later. I don't know because I had joined up later.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that in Podvelezje at the end of May 1992 there was an assassination against me?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An attempt?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, an assassination was carried out, but it was unsuccessful. A Muslim threw a grenade at me.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that Oliver was in Podgorica then?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally do not know that but I heard about it from the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Oliver Denis Barret was wounded then. He had wounds in the lower part of the abdomen and in his legs.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That was the reason for his withdrawal to Belgrade and for Vakic to come in his place. That could have been the reason if you don't know with any certainty?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know but of course if the man was wounded it is only reasonable for him to be withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: As for Ljubo Ivanovic the Serb Radical Party never sent volunteers to his unit. Do you have any information that they did?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You think that then in that terrain, somebody sent additional men.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. Because if Branslav Vakic was the commander and if part of our unit is at a forward post, if it is, he only could have done this through Vakic. He could have received replenishment or anything like that. I personally went from Grab to Podgorica to the railway station and I met people, all of this in coordination with the Montenegrin police and I brought them to the border. This was a few times. There were very few volunteers, but at any rate the Montenegrin police requested this kind of escort.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: However, if Ljubo Ivanovic left Vakic it's impossible for Vakic to send him replenishments. Isn't that logical?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it shouldn't be that way, but not a single clash of their interest is it grater than our common interest. I believe that if Ljuba had complained to him in any way, if he said that he needed help in terms of weapons or whatever, I mean, if Vakic was in a position to do that he would have done it and if I were in a position I would have done it too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: If Ljubo Ivanovic had lamented somewhere, saying, We are surrounded, help, everybody would have come to help him?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. You do not have any proof that Ljubo Ivanovic -- that the Serb Radical Party sent volunteers to Ljubo Ivanovic. That is important for me. In June your unit was engaged in Podvelezje and, at the same time, was there a unit of volunteers of the Serb Radical Party on the 13th of June that was operating in the territory of Mostar? Have you heard of such a unit?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the area of Mostar? On the 13th?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The 13th of June.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 13th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Here in the indictment it says that on the 13th of June there were volunteers of the Serb Radical Party. The so-called Seselj's men and the Serb forces were in action and among them there were some of Seselj's men too. Have you heard of any such thing?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything with any degree of certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Had something like that happened, you would have to know if you're a volunteer from that unit.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if it was our forward post, of course I would have to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you hear that there, in some of the villages that are called Zalik, Potoci, Put, Livac, Vrapcici, and others, 88 civilians were taken prisoner and that they were taken to the stadium in the village of Vrapcici, detained there and killed?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it possible that this was done by the volunteers of the Serb Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot make any assumptions because this is the first time I hear of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: First time. And their bodies were found in Borak at a garbage dump and some bodies were found in Sutine, I think, some were killed in Sutine and thrown into a pit by the Neretva. Have you heard of that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These names tell me that I never ever went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecution gave me a document, a document of the cantonal court from Mostar where it says that the indictment was issued against 30 Serbs, all them were locals from Mostar and the surrounding area, that is to say Herzegovina, and there's not a single one from Serbia. Is it possible that they were volunteers of the Serb Radical Party then?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Seselj is referring to a document and I was wondering if we could request that he identify the document that is he using, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Seselj, could you tell us exactly what document you're talking about? Where does this document come from? What is the date of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this moment I don't have it in front of me but this is a document that was provided to me by the Prosecution and it has one of their 65 ter numbers. It is the indictment of the cantonal Court in Mostar or rather the cantonal prosecutor's office in Mostar. They can find out straight away through their computers. I cannot carry everything around Judge. Look at all the packages I already have. If I were to carry everything that the Prosecution gave me, half of this courtroom would be packed. However, I am giving you the name of the document, a indictment against 30 Serbs who were suspected of having committed murders in Uborak and Sutine. The Prosecution gave me this key argument for wiping out this part of the indictment because there is not a single one of them who is from Serbia. If they find it, fine, if they don't, fine again. What matters to me is that this witness never heard of the crime in Uborak and Sutine and at the relative time he was there and he was in the volunteer unit, and I don't care about anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When you went out to Podvelezje, was Nevesinje by then already firmly under Serb control?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We stopped in the centre of town at a hotel. We had a rest -- had a coffee, had some -- took a rest and then we saw the unit of Colonel Medji [phoen]. I think that he was supposed to be something -- well, not our commander but he is a man who had to do some of the technical matters involved. He also gave us some radio communications for this action that we carried out as we were sitting in this hotel in the centre of town. Of course, the town was in Serb hands although it was full of refugees from Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Serbs?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Nevesinje was never under Muslim control, right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: From the very beginning of the war it was under Serb control incessantly, right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nevesinje, Ljubina, Trebinje, all of it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, the pace is too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The indictment says --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the exact reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The Serb forces took control of Nevesinje.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to make a comparison for you it would be the same thing if you were to say on such-and-such a date, such-and-such Serb forces took control over Banja Luka. It was always in Serbian hands. The population was Serbian, too, well, a certain percentage, but it is not that it was necessary to have any fighting for the city.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please be asked to slow down, interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's an important point I want to make. Seselj's men, who are in the indictment, I mean, many people refer to Seselj's men. You were on the field, so what exactly does this mean to you, this phrase, "Seselj's men"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite sincerely, many times, as I passed through Republika Srpska, and believe me I can list the names in Republika Srpska where I was not during the course of the war, so this has nothing to do with the volunteers of the Serb Radical Party in many other units within the army of Republika Srpska I was there. Then I would see a group of people in the street calling themselves Seselj's men. Never did I -- well, I was always skeptical. I know that a group would have to be organised by the Serb Radical Party. They'd have to have a facility given to them by the army, and anyway they had a different organisation. It wasn't that I -- the discipline wasn't that ideal but it certainly did not resemble the crowds I would see in the street, saying, oh, we are Seselj's men. Quite simply many people identified themselves in that way. I don't know why. Probably in the name of -- probably with the name of Mr. Vojislav Seselj that was very popular. So, just as I cannot identify a brigade in terms of it being from Posavina or Semberija and telling one soldier from another, I really could not identify, someone who'd belonged to a volunteer unit who operated in a particular area and called himself a Seselj's -- a man of Seselj's. I have to be honest about this. I personally never considered myself to be a man of Seselj's. I'm not fighting for Seselj. I simply believed that Seselj indicated something to me that I had not been aware of throughout history, that was a danger involved. I considered him to be my political leader in the sense of my future victory in the war and I thought that he was the representative of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, we see that a radical is going to become the president of Serbia, not I, but my deputy Tomislav Nikolic is going to be the president of Serbia. He's only a step away. Isn't it not possible that there were some self-styled groups that introduced themselves as Seselj's men, ten or 15 people would get together and say, We are Seselj's men. Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is not that they proclaimed themselves that but the locals would call them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Maybe they themselves did that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, maybe they themselves did that too. These emblems, the Serb Chetnik Movement, Racak, say at a check-point you'd stop and you could buy lots.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Perhaps somebody just wore spectacles and they thought that this person would have be a man of Seselj's?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. He'd have to be smart too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Or perhaps he would have to weigh 120 kilograms?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you hear that the Serb forces in the area of Velez took prisoner -- took 76 Muslim civilians prisoners and took them to Nopolje [phoen] in the area of Zijemlje to the elementary school. They separated the men from the women and children and killed them and their bodies were found in Teleca Lastva. Have you ever heard of any such thing?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did this happen in this war or in the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Supposedly in this war. I will tell you when. Around the 22nd of June.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Believe I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: They said were Serb forces and among them, Seselj's men?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Then it says that women and children were taken to the Kilavci heating plant in Nevesinje and that 44 of them were killed by a pit near Lipovaca. Have you ever heard of that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed. Mr. Registrar. Continue, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me finish before I forget. I listened to someone who was from that area and who was probably there in the relevant area, but -- at the relative time but I didn't hear of anything like that from him either.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you hear of this Lipovaca and women and children killed?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately in my work afterwards I did see women and children killed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, could the speakers please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're just too fast. The court reporter can't keep up, so that the answers are not recorded and neither are the questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall repeat, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it possible that volunteers of the Serb Radical Party participated in this, those who are called Seselj's men, without you knowing anything about that. Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whoever claims that that happened placed a date to it. You have already said and we have already seen masses of documents here when it was that we were in Grab and so on. Now I don't know whether all of that can be linked up. I as deputy commander at Grab have no idea about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: They even say that five women were transferred to the resting facility in the Konjic municipality of Boracko Jezero and that they were later killed there. And that this rest house was in the hands of the Serb forces, Seselj's men, and they used it as a military base. Did you ever hear of volunteers of the Serb Radical Party at Boracko Jezero, the lake of Borac?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, while I was there I heard of the lake, but I'm not saying that I heard of something like an Ovcara having happened there. Do you know what I'm saying? Well, maybe I even heard this through the communications, but I was never there. I cannot say anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you hear of Draskovic's Serb Guard being active there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did see the Serb Guard, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was there constant tension and animosity between our volunteers and the Serb Guard?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was no love lost between us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did Vakic ask for the volunteers of the Serb --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note that we could not follow the question.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spent two nights in Leotar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Please repeat the question. It was not taken up by the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Stoparic, that Branislav Vakic requested the mayor of Trebinje, Bozidar Vucurevic, to have the members of the Serb Guard under the command of Branislav Lajnovic, Dugi, be thrown out of Trebinje because of a lack of discipline; otherwise, they had been put up at the Leotar Hotel and they by behaved in a rowdy way?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was just about to answer before the judge interrupted because they didn't understand the question. Two or three times the commander would send me to Trebinje for something and I didn't have to go back straight away. He would give me an evening off, right? And then I would spend the night at the Leotar Hotel. That happened a few times. The Leotar Hotel was a base for soldiers that we called Draskovic's men. What the difference was between them and us was that they all had identical uniforms, insignia, that is to say that they a sponsor who bought this from them it is it not that the army it to them from a nearby brigade. They were much better equipped. As for some of their arrogant behaviour, I heard about that but quite simply I saw them there and it is not illogical that they behaved arrogantly because they were not engaged in intensive fighting. They were sitting there and looking for girls in town, so it is possible that there were different people there. I cannot remember the exact details, whether Branislav Vakic asked for them to be relocated or not. Even if that was the case, I would not be surprised to hear that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Drazilovic's men, were they JNA members or did they belong to a paramilitary unit or still to the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whether they had signed a loyalty oath to anyone is something I don't know. It would be very strange that somebody to gravitate there as a paramilitary next to the brigade command, but in that war everything was possible, so I don't know. I can't say. They took the best place for its base. We were sleeping in some dilapidated military institution high up, whereas they were in town with their cooks, kitchens, tea, coffee and so on. So were they the paramilitary, well-paid soldiers by someone, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday or the day before yesterday, I can't remember, you talked about command and control. I have a very simple question for you: These men, Drazilovic's men, who were they controlled or commanded by? You may know; you may not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Draskovic's men. Drazilovic is one man. Draskovic is something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They considered Vuk Draskovic to be his political leader and the SPO and they had their commanders, platoon commanders, many of them deceased now, people from the Belgrade underworld criminals and they were the people who established that army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This Draskovic man, who -- which political party or formation did he belong to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] His party was called the Serbian Renewal Movement, SPO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Party of Serb renewal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Have you heard, Mr. Stoparic, of the killing of 11 civilians, Muslims on the 26th of June, 1992 or around about that date from the area Rustak Luna [phoen], captured in Teleca Lastva, they were held and tortured in the primary school in Zijemlje seven were taken off and killed. Their bodies were found in the pit in Zijemlje. Have you had heard of that killing?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have never heard of those villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it possible that the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party took part in these killings without you knowing about it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if they were in my unit, then it would be impossible that I didn't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stoparic. Now, do you know, Mr. Stoparic, that Oliver Denis Barrett was an Albanian and that his real name is Mujo Bunjaku?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what his real name is but I did know that he was an Albanian. I even thought that when he was unfortunately killed in front of his house or something, that perhaps the Albanians had killed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It wasn't the Albanians who killed him. It was the Serb criminals, because he lived with the former wife of one of the mafia members. His name was Vaso Pavicevic, so he organised an ambush out of jealousy and that's how he came to be killed. So an Albanian was a Chetnik Vojvoda, as I proclaimed him. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now do you know that the mother of Branislav Vakic is a Hungarian lady?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Vakic never told you about that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps he did but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Have you heard of Radovan Novacic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Radovan Novacic was the commander of the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party in Western Slavonia, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't in Western Slavonia so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But did you hear of that, have you heard of him?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe later on if you add something, it might help me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Right. Do you know that Radovan Novacic was a Croat?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, in my unit, just to paint the picture what happened in my small platoon, which didn't number more than 25 men, it wasn't an ethnically Serb platoon. Many volunteers were from Novi Sad. Now, whether they Ruthenians, Slovaks, and even Croats, what their reasons were for coming there, for joining up as volunteers, I don't know, but we took them in, we accepted them and they didn't demonstrate in any way that they didn't deserve to be with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Does that mean that volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party did not display national intolerance at all?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's like this. I attended funerals in Backa Palanka, for instance, of the volunteers of the Serbian volunteers who were killed in Herzegovina. The names were Istvan, for example, and all the other Hungarian names and we had no pretensions vis-a-vis them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You mean tensions, not pretensions, you used the wrong word, I think.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's right. And even if I went somewhere else to another area, then later on I would mobilised him by ringing him up on the telephone and tell him where he would be. It's not an obligation. I'm just saying we're going into the area, into the field and if he wanted come to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Ante was the name of Radovan Novacic. Now, do the Serbs have the name Ante, not Antonije but Ante. Have you ever heard of a Serb with the first name Ante?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Stoparic. Now let's briefly move on to the question of Brcko. Now, you were there, as you said during the examination-in-chief, you were the commander of the volunteer unit which was called the Novi Sadski or Novi Sad volunteer. We called it the 7th Novi Sad Volunteer Company and the military post and stamp that was devised in the barracks for us had the 7th Novi Sad Detachment on it. And that unit had nothing to do with the Serbian Radical Party except that some of its members might have been a member. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That particular unit had nothing to do with the Serbian Radical Party except, for example, Milenko Petrovic would organise something in the Sid municipality, organise assistance in the sense of cigarettes, clean underwear, not to bring it just to me but to the Brcko hospital, too, and that was political work on the part of the Radical Party in the form of assistance and so other -- well, not parties but sometimes - and I can't say that I didn't use my personal collections sometimes with Mr. Milenko and issue a cry for help and say, We need good men, have you got any and then he'd try and do something if all of his men hadn't gone off, because people who took part in the war had always been sent somewhere, so he tried to do something to help out, so we did have that type of cooperation but not officially. Officially we were not a unit organised by the Serbian Radical Party in Belgrade or [indiscernible] all the wartime staff of the Serbian Radical Party send volunteers to your unit, did it? We were duty-bound to take the IDs or military booklets of every person that volunteered, we would take it to the security officer, [indiscernible] Milenkovic, the brigade commander as well and then they would decide whether the man could be taken in or not and then I would take him into my unit. So many people were members of the Serbian Radical Party. Many were members of other parties. Many weren't members of any party. We would also take in from the people from Republika Srpska itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But nobody came officially as a volunteer of the Serbian Radical Party sent by our wartime staff. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: You have to observe the pause between answer and question. You will, as a lawyer, Mr. Seselj, recognise the importance of everybody being able to understand what is being said here. And, Mr. Witness, please wait before you answer the questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue? At one point in time we also needed assistance, so a man by the name of Bakic -- and I would mix him up with Vakic. He was from Backa Palanka and he said that he was a radical, for instance. I know that several years ago when I saw him for the last time he was working in the customs office and he brought in a group of men from Backa Palanka and the surrounding areas. Now, whether they became informed in the party, the Radical Party office about that -- because that is possible too, you know, people would come into the offices and they said, Well, we have a hot spot over here so volunteers are needed and things like that and you will agree with me that you as the head of the radicals, you wouldn't mind where the volunteers went if they came of their own accord and wanted to go, if they were fighting on the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In this trial I want to distinguish between the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party that we sent from Belgrade to the front from any other volunteers so -- because this is a false indictment that I have to defend myself against, so I assume you understand that, too. Now you heard that Branislav Vakic took part in breaking through the corridor at Brcko, right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Branislav Vakic?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes. Do you know when the corridor was broken through?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards the end of May, I believe. When I arrived in Brcko the surrounding area of the hospital had already fallen and we thought, Ha, now we have a corridor, so before me, there was the Vojvoda from Bijeljina who was involved in that corridor. As to Branislav Vakic, I don't know. Quite possibly. Why not?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Branislav Vakic was there for a short time while the corridor fell and then he left the area. What was important? To link up the Banja Luka area with the rest of Republika Srpska, right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corridor was not only important for the people in Republika Srpska but it was an extremely important thing for the Knin Krajina area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: For the whole of the Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You mentioned Mirko Blagojevic and he was from Bijeljina, was he not?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned him in the sense of liberating the town of Brcko, before me, that is. He was there before me. Mirko Blagojevic's units were in Brcko before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mirko Blagojevic is from Bijeljina, is he not?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know he's from Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He's a member of the Serbian Radical Party, is he?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He ought to be, should be, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But the Serbian Radical Party from Belgrade never sent him volunteers, did it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that and I don't see why it should because he had enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: From Semberija, his own people, right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, during a time he was as strong as the Panthers, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You mentioned someone else, that unfortunate man, Goran Jelisic. Now, Goran Jelisic, to the best of your knowledge, did he have anything to do with the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, and how I got to know Goran Jelisic, I already had my office in -- well, we were given a whole pavilion, in actual fact. He stormed in one day with several other people and asked that we take him in as volunteers in my unit, and I was informed, as is customary, the security officer about that. He was Major Krstic. He agreed, of course, I took him in. But he was just there for two weeks and then he left and then he turned up with some Arkan fighters and he paraded through town. Now I don't know that he can have anything to do with the Radical Party at all. I don't think he is a member of the Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you hear that he acknowledged in front of this Court that he had killed 16 prisoners in the prisoner camp lorry in Brcko? What was the name of the camp?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Luka, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, I meant Luka camp in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't hear him owning up. I heard a lot of that before, about that before. I read the judgment because it was interesting because I knew him personally, and I read the judgment of Dragan Ivanovic [as interpreted] too. That's all I know about this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes. Right. Is it possible that those killings in the Luka camp can have anything at all to do with the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he said that Biljana Plavsic appointed the chief of that camp or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He mentioned Biljana Plavsic, did he?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I read about it all a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Stoparic. Let's not dwell on the question of Brcko any more and move on. Now we have a very interesting area, an interesting question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you planning a break, Mr. President, now or ... because I have another area to cover, a set of questions which will take up a little more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We should have had the break in five minutes time, but we can have it now. It is 20 to 4.00. We'll start again at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing can resume. I will give the floor to Mr. Seselj to continue with his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, I'm going to have a few unpleasant questions for you now, but I suppose you expected that of me, I'm sure, right? It's not taking you by surprise. Now, after your warfaring in Brcko, according to your statement, and I'm quoting your statement, the one you gave to the Prosecution, let's see what paragraph. Perhaps it is not essential but we'll find it if need be. Anyway, somewhere near Teslic --

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: If the witness is going to be questioned on his statement I request that he be given a copy of it. This is actually the original, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Seselj, if you ask a question he should have the document right before his eyes. It would be easier.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I won't, Judge. I'd just like to remind him -- well, I didn't know about this earlier but I'd like to remind him that he said himself to The Hague investigators that after the war in Brcko, near Teslic he moved with a group of Serbs, he crossed over on to Croatian territory and fought with the Croats against the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the absolute truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: True, right. Then we don't need to look at the statement.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I have to give you a explanation because it wasn't literally changing over to the HVO, Croatian Defence Council. It was a cooperation by the brigades, the Serb forces, whole Serb forces were in Zepce and that's near Zavidovci. And so from Teslic from the school facility there and at the time it was used as the seat of the military police in Teslic, I was sent there, attached to a brigade, a company there, where, in joint action -- it wasn't the Croatian army there. It was the Croatian Defence Council there, just to paint this image of how close our actions were, they -- we slept one house next to the other and then we would make an evening dinner together, barbecue together.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, that means you went there on assignment, does it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: By -- on orders?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with Serbian insignia and together with the HVO because there was the danger, which is something I learned afterwards, there was the threat of -- well, I like to joke about this and say that the love between the Croats and Muslims dissolved and then there was the danger that from Zavidovici and even Zenica, large Muslim forces destroy that Croatian enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is that the Medzik enclave?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's Zepce.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Right, Zepce. And how long were you fighting there for?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A little under a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And that was in 1992, was it, towards the end of 1992?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date. It was autumn. There wasn't any snow, so if it were already winter, it would have been snow, there would have been snow over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Then late autumn?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that I went from Brcko with some 20 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How long did you stay there for? Yes, I will make pauses. I have been cautioned again. How many days did you stay there for?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Less than a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And did they pay you for your military involvement there? Did you receive a salary of any kind?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was it from the Croatian side or was it a regular salary from the army of Republika Srpska that was paid out to you?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: The interpreters made a request to have the witness repeat his answer to the question of whether he was paid for his military involvement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
