utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. Line 19. Mr. Seselj, you were so fast in your question that we did not get the answer. Could you please ask the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stoparic said that in Brcko he was paid out for that part of his military involvement. Now I'm interested in hearing whether it was a regular salary as a soldier of the army of Republika Srpska or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hold on, Mr. Seselj. Mr. Stoparic said he was paid at the Brcko barracks, but when he was answering, he was answering a question, a question that you asked on line 19 at 16 hours and some seconds. But the question was not recorded on the transcript, so ask the question again, please. Ask him, Were you paid for that period of time? Or I'll ask the question myself. We have a problem with the transcript. It is not on the transcript. So, Witness, please, were you paid at the Brcko barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not receive a salary at all on -- in the area of Zepce but in Brcko and it wasn't anything that was explicitly calculated for that period of time. The end of the month came, the beginning of the next one, and it was time for my salary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So if I've understood you correctly, you received the same salary as you would have done if you had spent all that time at Serb positions within the framework of Serb forces in Republika Srpska, right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. No bonuses or extra remuneration of any kind. We would make jokes later on because we had two or three men who were lightly wounded, luckily, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, this is very complicated. Judges are jurists and they will have to make decisions according to what you're saying and according to the questions and the evidence and we're certainly discovering that -- that you participated to a military operation against the Muslims with the HVO. So the question that springs to mind is, to which army it belonged, JNA, Republika Srpska, some kind of autonomous unit, military unit? What country, what command were you under at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer? I believe, Mr. President, that you're confused on account of some facts and you will be even more confused when I tell you that I was also later with the Muslim army in this war. What I'm something now is that I was a member of the army of the Republika Srpska of the Semberska or the 2nd Semberija Brigade. This was agreed at a higher level by the Serbian authorities and the military command with the Zepce enclave in which there was a brigade of not the HVO but the Croatian Defence Council and we helped them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before that, we had been enemies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you were with Republika Srpska. But was it the JNA that had told you to join Republika Srpska? What happened? I remind you that you had a military booklet that normally you were a soldier of your country and the official army of your country was the JNA. And suddenly you're telling us, fought for Republika Srpska. So I'm trying to understand. How could you shift from the JNA to the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, Your Honour, at what particular moment the JNA left the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Republika Srpska set up its own army which was called the army of the Republika Srpska just as the other side had established its own army and the Croatian portion of the people had their own Croatian Defence Council. In Brcko I signed what was given to me, a batch of documents by the mayor. Ristanica, it involved dual nationality, and I was recognised in nationality of Republika Srpska and my own citizenship of the Republic of Yugoslavia. On that basis I voluntarily became a member of the army of Republika Srpska and was the commander of the unit which was called the 7th Volunteers, Novi Sad Company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On your military booklet, I did not see that mentioned. Why is there no entry of this on your military booklet?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have Mr. Stoparic's military booklet here in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you moved to Republika Srpska, normally there should be mention of this, that you were placed with this Republika Srpska at one point in time. This Republika Srpska that would set up within Bosnia and Herzegovina and there is no mention of this in your booklet. Can you explain why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you give this military booklet to me and put it on the ELMO here, I will show you that it does exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here is your booklet.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honour, it's 65 ter exhibit number 32.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, as we are by now already discussing a document which was submitted by the Prosecutor, I do hope that you will add that much time to the time remaining available to me for my cross-examination because every minute is precious to me, believe me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But you raised the problem in the first place and it is absolutely normal that we should look into it. Either we just consider that what you are saying is of no value so we are doing all this exercise in your interest. Otherwise, you know, I can just hand that document back to the Prosecutor and you can have your own time. I don't really understand, you know, this problem with the allotment of time. You raised a problem. We're trying to look into it to see whether or not the soldier at the time depended on you or not. It seemed that it did not because he was in Republika Srpska. This is what we're checking at the moment. Witness, please, you had the stick in hand at the moment. Could you show us with that stick the seal of Republika Srpska in the booklet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, Mr. President, all these stamps here, can you see the difference between this type of stamp and this type, the other type of stamp in terms of their sizes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is the stamp which I received for a terrain organised by the Serbian Radical Party in Bubanj Potok. The JNA is authenticating that I was engaged during that period in that particular terrain. That's it. It is 1992. Is it not according to the rule actually above this where we have the year 1993 indicated. It doesn't really matter whose stamps these stamps but not always stamps were actually stamped in the booklets. One was given certificates. This stamp says military PO, post office 7400, Brcko and this one is different. The other one is of the army of the Republika Srpska, from Brcko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you're saying that the stamp on the right-hand side, the second one on the right-hand side, is the stamp of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This one in the second line in the second row, that is the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army stamp. Can I be of assistance, Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Yugoslav People's Army, according to its regulations, exclusively used the Latin script as the script for official communication, and the army of Republika Srpska uses the Cyrillic script, and it is already on that basis that you can distinguish between a stamp that comes from the JNA and the one deriving from the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So to end this, could you show us with the stick which one is the stamp of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So they're five all together. And the one in the top, in the middle is the one from the People's Army of former Yugoslavia, is that it?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the record, this is page 27 in the e-court document. It has been marked for identification as exhibit 22.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now let's get the military booklet back so that we can hand it over to the Prosecution, and Mr. Seselj can have the floor to continue with his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, it was important for me just to have you confirm the allegation that for a while you fought on the part of the Croatian army, on the side of the Croatian army against Muslims, and now you describe the circumstances. You stated that in the beginning of 1993 you actually excluded from the Serbian Radical Party, is that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I said that I was excluded from it. Whether I mention that particular date, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In paragraph 122 of your statement of the 1st, 2nd, 3rd and 4th of August, 2006 in The Hague, paragraph 122 it is stated that: In 1993, after the Brcko campaign, I received a letter at my address in Sid from the Serbian Radical Party's regional board for Srem and in that letter you were informed that you were expelled from the Serbian Radical Party. Do you confirm that statement which you gave here to the investigators of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I confirm that that was the way in which I was expelled from the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In another place somewhere else you said that you had you forgotten the reasons and here you stated that it was written in the letter that your conduct was not correct, that you did not behave correctly, that you were not in line with the party and that you obstructed the work of the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Remember precisely, it was obstructing the work.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes. Now follow me carefully. Was your expulsion associated with the fact that we learned that you had fought with the Croats against the Muslims, was that the reason why you were expelled from the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I apologise for addressing you personally. It is quite clear to you yourself that I did not fight on the side with the Croats. It was in concerted action for the sake for some loftier aims which emanated from the agreement reached between the Republika Srpska and the Zepce enclave. I was wearing the insignia of the Republika Srpska as a Serbian soldiers. Even the Croatian soldiers greeted me, Good morning, Serbian soldier.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please do not overlap.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I shall remind you now, Mr. Stoparic, at the time when the conflict erupted between the Croats and the Muslims, do you know that I publicly advocated the position that the Serbs should reach agreement with the Muslims against the Croats and that the leadership of the Republika Srpska actually pursued a policy of an alliance with the Croats against the Muslims? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may have been so. You may have advocated that particular position but I was a member of the army of Republika Srpska, an officer of the army of the Republika Srpska according to orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm not disputing that but that was directly opposite to the policy pursued by Serbian Radical Party. Let me remind you of another thing. At that time I went to Pale to talk with Radovan Karadzic to try and persuade him that a much better solution was to try and reach an agreement with the Muslims and with Izetbegovic and not with Boban, rather than with Boban Bobanj and the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, which is what Karadzic actually did with Mate Boban. I talked on TV Pale, the state television of Republika Srpska and I presented this position of mine, saying that it was in the Serbs' interest to strike an alliance with the Muslims and not with the Croats. Are you aware of that, did you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I waited for the translation. I know one thing. This is exactly happened. We Serbs struck an alliance with the Muslims and I personally was in the area of Velika Kladusa where I trained Muslims. I assisted Muslims in concert, in coordinated action in this fight against the 5th Corps of Alija Izetbegovic. Also with the Croats I -- when the position was changed I participated with the Muslims in a fight but not against the Croats but against the Muslims again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But this is something else, Mr. Stoparic. There, you were on the side of Fikret Abdic against Izetbegovic's army, right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fikret Abdic had seceded and created his own enclave in Krajina had his own army which we wholeheartedly supported and we fought against the notorious 5th Corps and even more notorious brigade whose --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Which -- the name of which the interpreter could not hear because of the overlap.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I'm observing that Mr. Seselj is interrupting the witness's answer and that there is again overlap that is preventing interpretation. I would like to be able to follow the evidence being presented to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, let the witness finish his answers. His answers are quite elaborate and long, and if you cut him off he cannot finish his train of thought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One observation, something that we need to understand things better. Witness, when you're talking about the Serbs, I don't understand whether you're talking about the Serbs from Serbia, that was still the Federal Republic at the time, or whether you're talking about Serbs from Republika Srpska. Could you please make that specific every time? You belonged to a unit of Republika Srpska, and you continued to the end to belong to a unit of Republika Srpska? Is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Judge, when I refer to the Serbs I'm referring to all Serbs. In the period under consideration I was a member, in fact, an officer of the army of Republika Srpska. That is what I'm talking about. I didn't quite get it, whether I remained a soldier of the Republika Srpska until the very end, no, I belonged to another formation which may have belonged to the same group. They may have been units from Krajina or some other units from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. Something else now. You're saying that at one point in time, because of an agreement that occurred higher up, you cooperated with the Croatian Defence Council of Bosnia-Herzegovina against the Muslims, the Bosnian Muslims. You confirmed this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is absolutely true, and I'm surprised of the fact that this is mentioned for the first time in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But that was in the framework of cooperation and not under the command of the Croatian Defence Council. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Zepce area, in that little town proper there was a command of the Serbian forces with a general and there was a huge house set aside for that particular purpose where the Serbian flag was hoisted. Some 500 metres away from that there was another just as huge house with the Croatian flag flying and a Croatian general in charge. That was on their terrain. They were actually occupied, although we did not engage in any combat with them. After this cooperation had ended we withdraw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, I come back to what Mr. Seselj was saying. He made a speech in Pale where very openly he opposed Karadzic, who wanted to join the Croats against the Muslims and in Mr. Seselj's speech - we don't have it yet but we may have it some day - Mr. Seselj is opposing this idea. Did you -- how did you hear about this speech among all the Serbs that were there? Was there a discussion about all this? Because there was really a problem of substance here. There was cooperation with HVO while, at the same time, high -- higher officials of Serbia were of the opposite opinion, and so this could lead to complications within your unit and maybe breakups. So did this speech of Mr. Seselj have any incidence or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Cooperation at least in the Zepce area was severed in less than a month. So my actual involvement lasted for about three weeks and it was not resumed later. It is possible that Mr. Seselj had influenced the political and military leadership of Republika Srpska to change the decision, but what had happened had happened. There was side-by-side cooperation. We fought side by side. It may now sound absurd, whereas a day before that, we had shelled one another. Politics; that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're saying that the day before you were shelled and then the day after you were -- you agreed to attack another enemy. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, yes, perhaps I am portraying of sort of caricature of the events. Of course, these negotiations lasted for sometime before that. When we arrived there with our hardware and our technical equipment they assigned us to some quarters where we could stay. They gave us - the Croats, that is - their own houses where we could be billeted. We were shelled by the Muslims from Zavidovici and I believe that we had a joint action targeting the Krivaja-Zavidovici plant which was a pre-war large manufacturing plant. Actually what I know, we did fight side by side with the Croatian fighters, and there were anecdotes about the -- some of our wounded fighters who would go to the military hospital to be treated. Their actual discharge papers from the first medical facility where they had been treated in Zepce had the chequered flag, the stamp with the chequered Croatian flag.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: According to what you have just now said, you spent a maximum of a month, participated for a month in this alliance between the Serbian and Croatian forces against Muslims?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I could see here, the alliance was broken at the initiative of the brigade from Bosanski Brod. We know how much they suffered at the hands of the Croatian army, and they could not agree to fight with them side by side, so it all started quickly, ended quickly. We get out of that terrain and left them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, that could have been something of a local nature. However, I am reminding you that the war conflict between the Croats and the Muslims and the Serb leadership of Republika Srpska firmly stood by the Croats. It lasted much longer all the way up to the Washington accords between Izetbegovic and Tudjman. Remember that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that are you right, Mr. Seselj. I'm talking about the Zepce area, but this cooperation went on for a long time in the territory of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And not only Mostar but also in Central Bosnia in some parts there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The Serb army was saving the Croats in Vares, right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard something about that, but I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: They sent hundreds of buses to get the Croats out who had been under Muslim pressure?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We usually did help the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now I wanted to put a brief question to you, only because you did not state anything specific here, what it was that was improper in your behaviour, why you were not towing the party line, why were you impeding the work of the party, why you were expelled. Your participation in the official alliance between Republika Srpska and the Croat community of Herceg-Bosna against the Muslims. I'm not accusing you because you went there. Do you understand me? You took part in that there as a soldier of the army of Republika Srpska. However, in this way, did you violate the party policy, that a decision therefore had to be made regarding your expulsion? I'm asking about that. I hope that I said all of this slowly enough.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, Nikola Vasic, who was then an MP by then, a Member of Parliament, an important person in the municipality of Sid and the Serb Radical Party there, at one meeting he accused me of cooperation with the DB. Perhaps that has something to do with it, although I don't know of anything to do with the DB. And quite simply, after that, it wasn't only me. Other people, too. I mean, there was this purge, and things have remained the same way to this day. However, there was this obstruction of work. And -- now was it Nikola or whoever signed that that did not go into this further, it is possible that I could have known about this because I was allowed to appeal the decision with the Main Board, so that's it. I mean I'm not saying Nikola Vasic or you or the Main Board. I'm not saying that you were guided by that. I mean, precisely what you were saying just now. I mean, I cannot. I personally, I mean I have not quarrelled with anyone personally there. It is not that someone would have expelled me for personal reasons. I don't see that possibility. Well, quite simply, the reason was as far as I can remember now, obstruction of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, does that mean that you do not recall or that you think that you were not told explicitly that your participation officially in the Croatian Serbian alliance in Bosnia was the reason for your expulsion. You cannot confirm that that was specifically stated?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot. I can remember an exchange of views with Nikola Vasic that he was accusing me of cooperating with the state security in Serbia. In what sense, I don't know. I didn't want to listen because I thought it was stupid. Well, yes, later on I was in the units of the state security but that was a lot later. So the real reason, believe me, Mr. Seselj, believe me, after the expulsion --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know what the reason was, but I dealt with it. I was an invalid for two years and it took me two years to realise that I was no longer a healthy person and then it took me two years to realise that I was no longer a radical.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You cannot confirm that this was the reason for your expulsion?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can not confirm or deny it.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I would like the witness to be asked to repeat his answer about what happened after the expulsion because the interpreter didn't understand the witness's answer and I think it should be placed on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. After the expulsion, what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that after I was expelled quite simply I needed a certain period of time to have my wounds heal, if I can put it that way. It took my two years to realise that I was an invalid, for instance, after I had been wounded and also when I was expelled from the party, it took two years for that wound to heal, and I'm not saying that I did not vote for Mr. Seselj's party twice in the elections. So it took me a long time to come to terms with the fact that I was no longer a radical. And as for the reason what Mr. Seselj is saying now, that does make some sense but I do not remember that somebody put it that way to me and also I am surprised that somebody knew at about me having taken part in such actions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as you know, are there other comrades, other friends of yours from that unit that was fighting the Muslims with the Croats who were also expelled from the Serbian Radical Party or were you the only one to be in that situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Out in the terrain, I always call it that when we go out into action, when we acted in coordinated fashion in Zepce with the Croatians there was this acquaintance of mine whose name I didn't know and I don't remember the other people and I don't think they were from Serbia, either, so I don't know whether some of them were members or whether they had been expelled later on in their own towns. I never talked about it with anyone. For a while I was ashamed of that participation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if -- what you remember is that you received a letter saying that you had prevented or obstructed the work, the activity of the Serbian Radical Party. Is that the reason to be found in the letter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember the following sentence. Because of obstruction of work. Now, I don't know whether something else was mentioned in that letter. I was so angry, Mr. President, that I crumpled that letter. It hit me straight in the heart, as we Serbs would say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Maybe this was not put right here, not literally as you had put it. However, in your statement, in paragraph 122, it says that in the letter it said that you did not behave correctly, that you were not in line with the party and that you obstructed the work of the Serb Radical Party. That's the wording from this statement that was given to me by the OTP that is allegedly your statement. Does this correspond to the truth?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right now I used the word obstruction. Obstruction is precisely what you referred to just now. It is possible that in that interview I remembered better and put it right, and we're all aware of the fact that it is obstruction and what you read out is identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In order to cut this unpleasant topic short - I hope it was unpleasant for both you and me - let us state that you stated that you do not rule out the possibilities that that was the reason why you were expelled from the Serb Radical Party. You cannot remember precisely, but that may have been the reason?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since we know that your position was in opposition to that cooperation, I do not rule out the possibility that that was the way in which you punish people who took part in that cooperation even against their will.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stoparic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could you please be so kind as to tell me how much time I have left because I will have to regroup the issues I have left, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to ask the legal officer to tell us how much time has been used up by Mr. Seselj already. It's going to take a few minutes. In the meanwhile, you can continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, please before you move into private session, may I state my views with regard to the matter, if possible. Because, really, I think that there were too many private sessions so far anyway. The only guarantee of a fair trial is keeping this trial public and I have no interest in examining in private or closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, to avoid any misunderstanding that might create problems with the Trial Chamber later on, private session, its purpose is to protect individuals, be they victims or witnesses or people who might sooner or later bear the consequences of what was said earlier on publicly. Therefore, we need to be cautious. That's all. We don't want to prevent you or to deny you a public trial. It is just to protect individuals.(redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber has decided that should the accused address this issue, it should be addressed in closed session. So, Mr. Registrar, let's move into closed session. Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I please ask whether the broadcast has been redacted beginning with the topic that Mr. Seselj --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is being done.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, now you can put any question you want.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all once again, I strongly protest at this violation of the fairness of this trial that I'm being denied the elementary right to have a public trial although I guaranteed in advance that I'm not going to mention any names (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: (redacted), according to you statement you were deployed along the part of the front line towards Sarajevo, right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Something like that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How long did you say in the area?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also for a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: A month, right. Now along that long journey, route, were there any foreign observers who could record your passage that way?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Now, in the area you did not have any serious combat operations, did you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, that's not quite true. There were a operations going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But a little bit of sporadic fire?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we had some dead, so it's not just sporadic fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How many people killed?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One person was killed but there were some others who were wounded. There was heavy artillery preparation by the Foreign Legion, French Foreign Legion. It is a good thing that we were not all killed when they hit us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So the Foreign Legion used artillery and hit you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the French contingent and they were Legionnaires as far as we knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why were they shooting at you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because they were protecting that sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So it means that a member of your unit was killed by French fire coming from the French Legionnaires?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you went your own way and pursued your own private matters?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for a while I was not engaged militarily at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In 1999 on the eve of the US aggression you and the majority of the Skorpions were called to join the Serbian police reserve force, right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, the commander of the Skorpions himself with all these heroes of his and his body-guards came to my house and asked me to get involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you reported to the SAJ, the special anti-terrorist unit?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told us that we were part of the SAJ, that this had been already finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, the Trial Chamber has admitted your testimony in the Milosevic case and in that case, Mr. Milosevic asked questions on all these topics that you have addressed. I did not remember whether this was in closed -- in private or open session. I think it was in open session, so if this was done in open session in the Milosevic case, it should also be in open session in this case. Could you please tell me whether you testified about all this in closed, private or open session?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, my entire testimony in the Slobodan Milosevic trial was in open session. Had anyone tried, the Bench or the Prosecutor, to force me to give my testimony in closed session I would have stood up and left the courtroom immediately, irrespective of any threatening consequences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I got the message.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Let's move back into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would have something else and now I cannot assess on the basis of that decision of yours whether it should be done in public or secretly. So don't be surprised. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: So it's up to you to do it the best way possible. If we realise, then, that something is wrong, we can address the issue and retrieve the situation as it happens. But let's move back into open session. You are very experienced when it comes to investigations and questioning; I realise that. You are very well aware of the import of what you do, what you say. Therefore, make sure that everything happens without any problem. Let's move back into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in now open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But then don't -- then don't, Mr. President, don't take it back now. I really do have to say now what it was that I had announced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go back into private session because obviously you failed to understand. Let's move back into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There are two ways to go about it. Either we tell you to put your questions, and we may think at some point that there is a problem, we would then move back into private session and redact. Or, we work in private session and we can lift the confidentiality depending on what would be said. As to the need for oral proceedings, I think the first solution is the better one for you. I don't know whether you understood me properly. I gave you an example. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Did you understand me now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand you, Mr. President. You do remember that a while ago, in principle, I accepted the qualification that I was the worst man in the world. However for the sake of legal history, and this trial will go down in that history, I want to leave the impression of proper gentlemanly behaviour even if I stand accused here. That is why I don't want to resort to any kind of trickery to impede the order that you establish here, not I. Sir, may I continue now?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, you know a bit of English, don't you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know what "trigger event" means?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know what a trigger is? A trigger is a trigger, like on a gun a pistol, an event is an event, right. So what would a trigger event be? In military terminology, it is a staged event, a rigged event that is used to justify, say, an aggression a military intervention. Hitler on the border with Germany organised an attack against his own gendarmerie, border police, whatever, and then he accused the Poles and on account of that carried out an aggression against Poland, right.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, after what happened in Srebrenica, in a way, NATO bombed some positions of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Let me remind you, not some positions but relentlessly for days, all of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also, after these events in Kosovo, NATO bombed the federal republic of Yugoslavia in order to prevent a further escalation of this as was stated publicly. I really don't know very much. I was never a spy or a counterspy, and I did not sit behind closed doors writing down what Kameni said or what somebody else said. That was not my job. And I don't like that. Sometimes I like to watch crime movies, but I'm not too thrilled. Now are we victims of an international conspiracy or a conspiracy of a group of several people? Sometimes when I was down there that's what I thought. However, now that I'm abroad. Well I was never ashamed to say that I was a Serb, but it is very hard for me precisely because I have very little information. As a simple man I can just say that I have my suspicions. So I'm sort of in between. I cannot say yes, it is possible, and I cannot say no either because I'm not a person who will say, Yes I'm 100 percent a victim of an aggression. And, on the other hand, when I look at some of the things that many people said, not only you, I really start doubting things. Do you accept this as an answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, you know this command structure of the Skorpions very well, don't you? You know them very well, and you know the luxury and the wealth they live in, right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: This wealth could not be obtained through a soldier's salary no matter how big it is?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a good salary but you cannot really buy a Ferrari and there were Ferraris.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I have a problem, because now and not just now you've done this for a long time. You're now being a witness yourself, you're testifying yourself. So please go back to asking questions of witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, a few moments ago I was answering your question. I was not testifying in my own trial. You asked me something, and I gave you an answer, why it was that I was insisting on these facts. And I reminded you that it was the witness who had spoken about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, maybe you could ask who is this Natasa Kandic. I don't know who it is. I have no elements on her. I have nothing on her. Could you remind us of who she is? Maybe the witness may help.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if ask you him the questions, Mr. President, I'm sure he'll tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't want to ask questions because then you're saying that I'm taking up your time. So you have all the time you were allotted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope that none of your interventions means deduction from my time, that it is deducted from my time. If I'm right, well, tell me, put me right. It is not deducted? Well, if it is not deducted, then I'm jeopardised as the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me tell you, when you are allotted one hour, you have one full hour. But if Judges take the floor during that hour, this is not deducted -- this is not taken into your time. This is deducted from your time. So you will have -- if you were given one hour, you will have one full hour for questions and answers, and when Judges take the floor this is not part of your time, which means that I investigate and ask questions on Kandic for five or ten minutes, you will not be deducted these five or ten minutes, and I would much rather that you go into the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps the interpretation wasn't correct. I was told that it would be deducted from my time if you ask the question; whereas earlier on I understood it that whenever you asked the questions, that time is not deducted from my time. So which is it? Is it not deducted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The truth -- you know, the truth is that when a Judge asks a question, this is not part of your time. This is not deducted from your time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that is counted as my time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, yes, this is your time because you're asking questions. Let me tell you how things work, Mr. Seselj. Ms. Dahl used up some five hours and some minutes, and you will have the same amount of time; five hours and 32 minutes. When Judges ask questions, the time taken for those questions is not part of those five hours and 32 minutes, which is why this hearing will go beyond the five hours and 30 minutes. When I ask questions, this is not taken out of your time. This is Judges' time and not your time. You have five minutes and 32 minutes for questions and answers. Did you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I have understood you exactly. But before your last statement, this latest statement of yours, I was receiving the wrong interpretation. The interpreter was saying quite the opposite and you can check that out. The interpreter explained throughout that your interventions were deducted from my time. You can check that out. You have a service to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was just an error.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to ask Mr. Stoparic who Natasa Kandic is.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Natasa Kandic is the president of the fund for humanitarian law in Belgrade. She has office in Belgrade, Novi Sad, Pristina and Podgorica. And probably in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That fund is officially a non-governmental organisation. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Officially a non-governmental organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you know that that fund received enormous financial notations [as interpreted] from the western governments and non-governmental organisations?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People said that it was Soros financing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Soros most of it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. You wanted to say that the question was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... in the creation of the record, and I think that the witness and the accused have resumed a very fast pace and should be reminded to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Remember, that when you speak too fast, you see that there are these little triangles that show up on the screen, showing that the answer was not recorded, or the question was not recorded; for example, on line 24. So please start again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I asked you whether you knew that the fund for humanitarian law, in formal terms, is a non-governmental organisation which is led by Natasa Kandic it is financed from western sources, the western governments, and non-governmental organisations. And your answer was that, as far as you knew, most of the funding came from the Soros foundation. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know this all from the media. I don't know it personally.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, sir, Mr. Stoparic, we're now going to broach a new question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I think we could go back into open session, Mr. President, if you agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Public session -- open session, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in now open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, you mentioned during the examination-in-chief -- I'm not going to mention any names, so you don`t have to ask for closed session. I'm not interested in names. I don't care about names at all. That members of the Serbian Radical Party in the 1990s took part in the persecution of Croats in Kukujevci. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, I did speak about that, but not as a witness but as somebody who listened, heard about that from other people, and I said what I remembered.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You mentioned the Croatian family of Kopoci in Kukujevci, right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes K, Kopic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And according to your statement a group of the Serbian Radical Party arrived at the Kopic house, Kopic family's house and persuaded them to leave Kukujevci, right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I repeat that I did not talk to any Kopic family person. It's what I heard about from you know who.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, and I'm not going to mention names. Now I investigated this statement of yours. You know that I have people who help me, whom I can rely, who are very reliable, and I myself received an enormous amount of material from the Prosecution. And now I know that the Prosecution will regret having sent me some of those documents. This is a book called "How My People Died." Have you ever heard of this book? This is a photo copy, unfortunately I don't have the original?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: May I ask Mr. Seselj to please read out an identifying mark. It is not visible in the record to hold up photocopies. We need to know what he is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This book, are you going to tender it into evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm sure it will be offered up to you by the Prosecution. But, on the first page of this document it says -- there is an ERN number, 01141837. The author of the book is Marko Kljaic, the Vicar of the Roman Catholic Church in Petrovaradin. You know that Petrovaradin is part of Novi Sad. It is the outskirts of Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Anyway, he wrote a big book, published it, and he devoted it Dr. Franjo Tudjman, that's the inscription, who was the president of Croatia, right? It's dedicated to him you can see that on page 5 of the book. Now that book has a total of almost 500 pages. On page 277?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- Which has the following number --

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... 65 ter number 02154 so that the Bench may follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: On page 277 of that book, and the ERN is 01142103, it says, there's a heading there. A list of expelled Croats from Kukujevci from 1991 to 1994. And this list contains 332 names, and it takes up a full eight pages. Of course, just not to have any misunderstanding the book is highly tendentious, and it is my thesis that not a single Croat was expelled from Serbia or Vojvodina as part of Serbia. Now he compiled a list in fact of all the Croats who, from 1991 to 1994 left Kukujevci. Do you wish to have a look at that list perhaps there is not a single name of Kopic on that list. No one by the name of Kopic on that list and you have the list on your screen.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't need to see the list. I understand what you're getting at. Perhaps I made a mistake. Perhaps the man wasn't from Kukujevci but from another village.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic for me to travel around Vojvodina looking for the Kopic family?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But we all know that these are villages bordering on each other so I might have made a mistake because the villages had the same structure as Kukujevci. So I confess if I said Kukujevci, not because you prove that the man's name isn't on the list, and the list need not be correct and that can be checked out where these Kopics were it wasn't just one family, one Kopic family so possibly they were in the other village, Veberac.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So I'm going to have to check out Veberac overnight, Mr. Stoparic, you're going to force me to do that, but I have a list here of expelled Croatian families from Geberac; however, this relates to 1996 and what was this man Kopic's first name?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The father was Ivica Kopic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I see, Ivica Kopic from Gibarci, Cepin, that's part of Gibarci, is it, possibly.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's Titova 10 Street, Titova Street Number 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether's Titova 10. That's what it says here, Titova Z. I found it that I found Ivica Kopic in the list from Gibarci, so you partially right. But the Catholic priest, Marko Pijajic, who did this very neatly and pedantically with respect to the Croats that moved out, said that this was according to the 1996 census. That's what he based it on. Kopic, Ivica, so he moved out and re-settled in Cepin, whereas he was in Gibarci, Titova Street, which means he wasn't from Kukujevci. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that I had my doubts whether he was actually from Kukujevci.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Right, then he went to Cepin, and Cepin is a place in today's Croatia?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is too, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He exchanged his property for the property of some Serb family?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Nowhere in this book which represents a detailed list and description of the various incidents did I find the fact that in his yard somebody threw a hand-grenade?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand what you want to say, what you're saying. When I mentioned a hand-grenade, I didn't claim that I was close by and saw it. I just learned about it from somebody else so that this whole story about Kukujevci, Gibarci, and so on is something that I can categorically say is not based on my own personal knowledge, and I apologise; but Mr. Seselj you'll agree that if somebody tells a lie 100 times it become the truth, so in my statement there might be a truth which is not something that I conceived it wasn't thought up by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Does that mean that are you retracting your statement according to which the members of the Serbian Radical Party in a certain way through persuasion and so on and later on by throwing a hand-grenade forced Ivica, what was his name, Kopic to move out of Gibarci. That's not from Kukujevci anymore. It's not in Gibarci. Are you retracting that as unreliable?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said all the time that this is something that I heard from others. The only thing that I can say is reliable is what I can claim that I saw with my very own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So what you said in this courtroom is not reliable, is that it? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was I interrupted by you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, could you give us the paragraph of the witness's statement that's involved here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was in the examination-in-chief. I cannot tell you right now. I do not have the transcript before me. I'm not talking about his statement. I'm talking about the witness's testimony here in the courtroom. I stopped looking just at his statement. I believe we have agreed that everything in his statement is untrue, because he failed to repeat most of it here in the courtroom. So I'm basing my questions on what he stated in the courtroom only because his statement is totally out of place because if I were to list everything which is in the testimony and does not correspond to his testimony in court, we could go on all day for hours on end discussing it. I'm not interested in his statement as such anymore because it is no longer a posit to my case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Looking at the statement, I note that the Kopic family is mentioned on paragraph 86 as well as 87. That says in 1992, in Gibarci, the Kopic family was targeted by the Black Troika, et cetera. So, witness, you have the statement in front of you. Ms. Dahl gave it to you earlier. So what you're saying there at paragraph 86 is this hearsay, did you hear that from someone else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It should be read in total it should not be extract from its context. I never said, Yes, I was there, and I saw that but always including in my interviews with the investigators, I just related my information because the investigators ask you do you have information and whether you had learned of some things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in now open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now that we're in open session, you seem to have used up three hours and 50 minutes. All together you had been allotted five hours and 32 minutes so just do the math. All together you have about an hour and 30 minutes left tomorrow for the rest of your cross-examination. But we will recompute this accurately but you have about an hour and 30 minutes left. Once we're finished with the witness tomorrow, we will have a break, a 45-minute break for technical reasons because I will be on business elsewhere. We will have a break at 3.45 and resume at 4.30. Normally after this witness the expert Tomic is scheduled, so we will start with the examination-in-chief of Mr. Tomic tomorrow. And, of course, we will continue next week with that -- this other witness. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have a request and I should like to promise to you in advance that I will have such a request only in connection with the expert witness Theunens and perhaps another expert witness. I'm not going to abuse this in respect of regular witnesses but in respect of witnesses I need more than scheduled time. The Prosecution has allotted two hours for the examination-in-chief for the expert witness Yves Tomic and two for the cross-examination. I should like to ask you to allocate four hours to me for the cross-examination because I believe that this is a very important subject; this is the concept of Greater Serbia and it does require much more time to be discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In the decision we made on January 15, we decided to give you four hours. So we anticipated your request. So you will have four hours. Very well. Ms. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I think it would be appropriate to advise the accused that the Chamber also allocated four hours for the Prosecution, that way he can plan his preparations accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So, Witness, we will meet again tomorrow for the hearing in the afternoon, starting at 2.15. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 24th day of January, 2008, at 2.15 p.m. 22 23 24 25
